abstract: Variation in plant functional traits along climate gradients chiefly arises from two processes: turnover of species with different trait values, and trait adjustment within species across environments. Yet, the relative contributions of these processes remain poorly quantified, limiting our ability to predict how traits, species distributions and, in turn, ecosystem properties will respond to climate change. Across seven functional traits and 1867 plant taxa from continental Australia, we provide a unified assessment of among- versus within-species contributions across multiple dimensions of plant function. Species turnover emerged as the dominant process driving trait variation along both precipitation and temperature gradients. Nevertheless, the contribution of within-species adjustment to climate differed substantially among traits and was generally greater in non-woody than woody taxa, these patterns being most clearly expressed along precipitation gradients. Our findings imply that plant traits will track changing climatic conditions primarily through species replacement, particularly for traits such as wood density and seed mass. Species may also respond in situ through adjustments in leaf physiology and morphology and, in woody taxa, through shifts in relative allocation between leaves and stem tissues. This knowledge has potential to improve predictions of the structure and function of future plant communities.
